source: Knipper et al. (2025) The Bias is in the Details: An Assessment of Cognitive Bias in LLMs
finding: 45 models tested on 8 biases (anchoring, availability, confirmation, framing, overattribution, prospect theory, representativeness, interpretation). Nearly all show bias-consistent answers. Newer reasoning and API models resist more, but representativeness and anchoring stay the weakest spots.
numbers: 2,887,500 responses. Average bias resistance (1 = no biased answers): claude-3-7-sonnet 0.822, o4-mini 0.821, gpt-4.1 0.778, QwQ-32B 0.800, phi-4 0.736, Llama-3.3-70B 0.740, Qwen2.5-0.5B 0.427. Susceptibility range 17.8% to 57.3%. o4-mini: anchoring 0.786, representativeness 0.527, framing 0.810. gpt-4.1 representativeness 0.547, anchoring 0.656. claude-3-7 representativeness 0.719, anchoring 0.721. 56% of size gains come between 0.5B and 32B.
quote: larger models tend to exhibit lower susceptibility
limits: Vignette items with keyword-matched answers (biased / unbiased / unrelated), so not accuracy. Items may be public. No GPT-5 or Claude 4 class models. Temperature mostly 0.2.
agent_relevance: Frontier 2025 models still fail representativeness vignettes about half the time and anchoring about a quarter to a third. Put anchor and base-rate checks in the schema; framing and confirmation are mostly solved on these items.

source: Knipper et al. (2025) The Bias is in the Details (prompt-detail analysis, TELeR levels 1-5)
finding: More detailed prompts help only some biases. Level 2 (clear directive restating the task) is best for anchoring and confirmation. Levels 3-4 that tell the model to be rational, objective and fair raise resistance. Extra detail made overattribution worse.
numbers: Appeals to rationality: +6.5 to +14.9 points resistance. Availability up to +14.9. Level 2 gains on availability, framing, interpretation, prospect theory: 3.6 to 9.9 points. Overattribution degraded by up to 8.8 points. Abstract: size reduces bias up to 39.5%, prompt specificity up to 14.9%.
limits: Prompt levels differ in length and content, so tokens are not held equal. Effects are averaged over models and tied to the vignette family.
agent_relevance: A short directive plus a rationality instruction is a cheap first operator, but it is bias-specific and can backfire; test per bias.

source: Borjigin et al. (2026) AnchorBench: A Multi-Pathway Benchmark for the Anchoring Effect in LLMs (COLM 2026)
finding: Anchoring in LLMs depends on how the anchor reaches the model. Irrelevant anchors barely move four recent API models, but plausible anchors still do, especially via external text, retrieved documents and tool outputs. In-context metadata anchors do nothing.
numbers: 14 models (10 open, 4 API: GPT-5.4-mini, Claude Haiku 4.5, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Grok-3-mini), greedy decoding. Control Acc10 96-100% for the API models. Anchor influence on External suite, irrelevant vs plausible: GPT-5.4-mini 0.00 vs 0.14; Haiku 4.5 0.00 vs 0.12; Gemini 2.5 Flash 0.02 vs 0.07; Grok-3-mini -0.00 vs 0.16. RAG plausible 0.02-0.09. Open small models up to 0.43 (Gemma-4B External) and 0.98 (Qwen-1.5B History). Plausible anchors raise MAE by +3.6 (External) and +3.5 (Tool). Error-increasing shifts 29% vs error-reducing 23% (plausible only: 37% vs 20%).
quote: even frontier API models above 95% control accuracy remain susceptible to plausible anchors
limits: Numeric estimation items only. Small API models, not the largest. History suite uses a different control format; Tool effect depends on message format.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 partly closed: small frontier models resist irrelevant numbers but not plausible ones. The risk in agents is a plausible-looking number from a tool, retrieval or earlier turn. Add a source-and-independence check on any number the agent reads before estimating.

source: Borjigin et al. (2026) AnchorBench, Appendix A.16 mitigation headroom probe
finding: Simple prompt fixes for anchoring are inconsistent. 'Ignore extraneous numbers' helped, 'self-check for bias' made it worse, and chain of thought helped one model a lot and the other not at all.
numbers: Anchor discrimination (Disc) External, Qwen-7B / Llama-8B: baseline 0.26 / 0.30; ignore 0.16 / 0.10; self-check 0.45 / 0.28; CoT 0.14 / 0.31. RAG: baseline 0.20 / 0.16; ignore 0.14 / 0.04; self-check 0.30 / 0.11; CoT 0.03 / 0.08. Control MAE External Qwen-7B: 7.7 baseline, 5.0 ignore, 8.8 self-check, 1.1 CoT.
limits: Two small open models, two suites, no token matching, single runs. CoT output is far longer than the other arms.
agent_relevance: Design rule: ignore-the-number instructions and evidence-first estimation beat generic self-check. Self-check can raise anchoring. Test at equal tokens before adopting.

source: Huang et al. (2025/2026) Understanding the Anchoring Effect of LLM with Synthetic Data (SynAnchors)
finding: Anchoring is common across LLMs and shrinks with model strength and with reasoning mode, but does not vanish. SynAnchors is generated to avoid memorised classic items.
numbers: Share of questions showing anchoring (total): Qwen2.5-0.5B 60.5%, Llama-3.2-1B 57.1%, Mistral-7B 51.1%, Qwen2.5-7B 40.0%, GPT-4o-mini 37.0%, GPT-4o 27.3%, DeepSeek-R1 25.0%, Qwen3-235B thinking 22.0%. DeepSeek-R1 numerical relative error 0.114 (12.8% of items) vs GPT-4o 0.270 (29.0%). 100 samples per question for most models; 30 for some API models.
limits: Workshop paper; semantic and numerical tasks are synthetic. Ratio is a significance-based rate, not an effect size.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: reasoning models cut but do not remove anchoring on novel items (about 22-25% of items). Anchor control is still needed.

source: Huang et al. (2025/2026) SynAnchors, Table 2 mitigation strategies
finding: Conventional fixes barely change anchoring. The best one, a two-step 'set your standard first, then answer' prompt (Anti-DP), helped partly.
numbers: Llama-3.1-8B total anchoring ratio: baseline 34.7%; question-aware prompt 36.8%; knowledge enhancement 50.5% (worse); self-improving 38.4%; adversarial fine-tuning 33.3%; DoLa 37.5-38.5%; Anti-DP 24.7%. Qwen2.5-7B: baseline 40.0%; self-improving 48.0% (worse); Anti-DP 40.8% (numerical 50.0%). Paper states up to 10% alleviation.
limits: Two small models; Anti-DP not token-matched; LoRA arm uses test splits only.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: no prompt rewrite beat all alternatives consistently. A two-phase 'fix the criteria, then judge' step is the most promising but model-dependent.

source: Sovrano et al. (2025) Is General-Purpose AI Reasoning Sensitive to Data-Induced Cognitive Biases? Dynamic Benchmarking on Typical Software Engineering Dilemmas
finding: Decisions on realistic software engineering dilemmas flip when bias cues are added with the logic unchanged. Sensitivity depends strongly on bias type and rises with reasoning steps for most biases.
numbers: 8 biases, 6 models, three benchmark generators. Anchoring and availability sensitivity 5-12%; hindsight and hyperbolic discounting up to 70%. More inference steps raise sensitivity: anchoring +3.77 pp (CI 2.2-5.3), availability +9.81, bandwagon +8.84, confirmation +33.66, framing +23.10; hindsight -17.25, hyperbolic discounting -17.70. Seed set: 16 hand-written tasks.
limits: Cost-effective models only (GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4.1-mini, LLaMA, DeepSeek-R1 distill). Sensitivity = decision flips against the unbiased version of the same dilemma.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: for engineering decisions, framing and confirmation cues cost the most, and cost grows with task complexity. Multi-step planning is where bias checks matter most.

source: Sovrano et al. (2026) Mitigating Prompt-Induced Cognitive Biases in General-Purpose AI for Software Engineering (PROBE-SWE)
finding: Common prompt fixes (CoT, bias warning, impersonation self-debiasing) did not significantly cut bias sensitivity per bias. A different step, eliciting the best-practice axioms first and injecting them before answering, cut it about in half.
numbers: Median bias sensitivity: control 12.9%; IsD 10.2%; BW (bias warning) 10.3%; BW+IsD 8.3% (not significant per bias, all p >= 0.07 after FDR); axiomatic cue plus BW 6.3% (p < .001, rank-biserial 0.4-0.5). DeepSeek-R1 distill baseline 16.3%; CoT sometimes raised sensitivity. Average reduction about 51%, up to 73% for some biases. Hindsight is the exception. Open-ended check, 40 dilemmas: gpt-4o-mini 12.5 points lower (31% relative), llama-3.1-8b 0.40 to 0.30; CIs include zero.
limits: Models are low-cost (GPT-4.1-mini/nano, 4o-mini, Llama 3.1-8B, 3.3-70B, R1 distill); authors say frontier models are untested. The extra elicitation step costs more tokens than the baselines, so not equal-token.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 evidence for a new operator: elicit task axioms and best practices before deciding. Beats generic warnings and CoT here but is not token-matched.

source: Oh et al. (2025/2026) From Belief Entrenchment to Robust Reasoning in LLM Agents (formerly When Debate Fails: Bias Reinforcement)
finding: In strategic games, multi-agent debate amplifies the majority initial view whether or not it is right. Debate cannot recover an answer the model starts with a low chance of choosing.
numbers: All actions with initial consistency above 0.5 became more likely after debate (p(3) > p(0)), correct or not. Fitted model residual -2.5%. Fix (DReaMAD, diverse prompts plus prior knowledge): +9.5% accuracy over ReAct, +19.0% higher win rate than standard debate on MetaNIM Arena.
limits: Sequential combinatorial games, not judgment vignettes. 'Bias' here means the model's static prior.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: supports that homogeneous debate is a poor debiaser. Debate needs perspective diversity, not just more agents.

source: Ma et al. (2025) Judging with Many Minds: Bias Amplification and Resistance in Multi-Agent LLM-as-Judge
finding: Debate between LLM judges raises position, verbosity, CoT and bandwagon bias sharply after round 1 and the higher level persists. A meta-judge design resists better. A bias-free agent helps in debate but less in meta-judge.
numbers: DeepSeek-V3 position consistency fell from 0.82 pre-debate to 0.71 after round 1; similar for Llama-3.3-70B and GPT-4o-mini. Drop from round 0 to round 1 significant across all judge-critic pairs; no significant further rise later.
limits: LLM-as-judge on MT-Bench-style tasks, not human-style judgment problems.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 firmer for judge setups: debate amplifies. Use independent samples plus a separate meta-judge, and randomise order.

source: Lyu et al. (2025) Self-Adaptive Cognitive Debiasing (SACD), Tables 2-4
finding: Reflexion and multi-agent debate had some of the highest bias scores in a three-domain test (finance, medicine, law), above plain prompting in several cells. SACD's detect-analyse-rewrite loop had the lowest.
numbers: FOMC, Llama-3.1-8B average bias score: vanilla 0.3805, CoT 0.3425, Reflexion 0.3830, debate 0.5020, zero-shot debiasing 0.2965, few-shot debiasing 0.2970, self-help 0.2100, SACD 0.1570. Debate on gpt-3.5 FOMC 0.5155; Reflexion on PubMedQA with Llama-70B 0.5585. SACD average scores 0.03-0.157 (finance), 0.0425-0.179 (health), 0.04-0.1235 (law). Iterations (gpt-3.5, finance): 0.2070, 0.1460, 0.1175 vs vanilla 0.1648.
limits: Bias score is a treatment-minus-control gap, not accuracy; the paper poses an accuracy question (RQ3) but reports bias scores per iteration. SACD uses several LLM calls, so it is not equal-token with CoT. The authors wrote both method and baselines.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: the SACD result is now backed by two independent debate papers, though SACD itself is still single-source. Gap 2: an iterative rewrite beats CoT on bias gap; accuracy and token cost unmeasured.

source: Huang et al. (2026) CogBias: Measuring and Mitigating Cognitive Bias in LLMs
finding: Prompt-level debiasing works for response-position bias, does nothing for information-order bias, and backfires on judgment biases (base rate, anchoring, sunk cost, status quo). Position bias is very large in all three models.
numbers: GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.3-70B, Qwen2.5-72B. Baseline first-option selection 79.0 / 77.1 / 77.6% vs chance 36.8%. Order bias 30.0 / 56.0 / 66.0%. Judgment shift -4.3 / -7.7 / -2.7 pp. Debiasing effect: judgment accuracy -4.4% (backfires), info-processing -1.1%, social +5.9%, response position independence +40.5%. Same family order in all three models: response > information processing > judgment > social.
limits: Three mid-size models; preprint under review; computable-ground-truth items only.
agent_relevance: Gaps 7 and 2: much measured LLM 'bias' is position preference, which a prompt fixes. Real judgment biases resist or worsen with a generic debiasing prompt. Always randomise option order before measuring.

source: Huang et al. (2026) CogBias, probing and activation steering
finding: Bias directions are linearly readable and steering them lowers bias with little capability loss in Llama, more in Qwen. Steering is not available to a prompt-only scaffold.
numbers: Linear probes reach 99.8% (judgment), 98.2% (information processing), 99.2% (response). Steering effect correlates across architectures r(246)=.621, p<.001 despite near-zero cosine similarity (0.01) between bias vectors. Capability loss on 25 benchmarks: Llama negligible; Qwen up to -19.0 pp for judgment biases.
limits: Needs weight access. Contrastive probe design may find prompt differences rather than bias.
agent_relevance: Not usable for a scaffold-only agent. Evidence that judgment bias is a stable internal feature, not only a prompt artefact.

source: Weerasekara et al. (2026) Conditional Cognitive Biases in LLMs: How Biased User Turns Modulate In-Context Reasoning
finding: Merely adding any user turn changes measured bias versus zero-shot, so zero-shot benchmark numbers do not transfer to chat. Biased user content raises bias in 6 of 8 models, while explicit bias cues trigger alignment suppression in others.
numbers: 24,300 jury-validated prompts over 81 cells, 8 models. Zero-shot bias magnitude 0.342 (Gemma-2-9B) to 0.437 (Phi-4). Presence effect of a neutral user turn +0.086 for Llama-3.1-8B (about 25% of the zero-shot level); positive in 7 models (+0.019 to +0.086), negative in Claude-3.5-Haiku (-0.101). Anchoring and confirmation near zero across user-turn contexts; planning fallacy rises in all 8.
limits: Mostly mid-size and older models; bespoke bias metric.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: part of the 'instruction-tuned models are more biased' result depends on dialogue format. Test the scaffold inside the real chat format.

source: Xiao and Yu (2026) Cognitive Bias Signatures in Search-Equipped LLM Agents: A Stage-Resolved Analysis
finding: With real search tools, result order, a dead-end history and a wrong hypothesis supplied by the user each change what agents retrieve, open and conclude. Effects differ by model. Opening counter-evidence more often did not always raise accuracy.
numbers: 10 models, 1,000 synthetic search worlds. Qwen switch rate after failure: 100% with no history, 87% with a neutral history, 23.5% with a dead-end history (76.5 pp total drop). Wrong-seed accuracy loss up to +43.5 pp on one model, 3.6 to 17.4 pp for most. Seek-disconfirming instruction: one model +23.0 pp accuracy with +22.5 pp opening; MiniMax opens 7.0 pp more but is 10.5 pp less accurate.
limits: Synthetic worlds; exploratory interventions; mixed open and API models.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: closest to an agent task. Anchoring on first evidence, sunk-cost persistence and wrong-hypothesis confirmation cost real accuracy. A forced 'change path' operator after failure is supported; a bare 'open counter-evidence' rule is not.

source: Ghosh and Panday (2026) The Dunning-Kruger Effect in Large Language Models: An Empirical Study of Confidence Calibration
finding: Verbalised confidence is very high regardless of accuracy and only weakly tied to correctness. Weak models are the most overconfident; stated confidence cannot flag a trustworthy first answer.
numbers: 4 models, 4 datasets, 24,000 trials. Accuracy / mean confidence / ECE: Gemini 2.5 Pro 80.9% / 99.5 / 0.185; Claude Haiku 4.5 75.4% / 86.0 / 0.122; Gemini 2.5 Flash 70.9% / 97.9 / 0.272; Kimi K2 23.3% / 95.7 / 0.726. Confidence-correctness correlation weak (up to r = 0.175; Gemini 2.5 Pro r = 0.011, p = 0.406).
limits: Single prompt format; the Dunning-Kruger label is an analogy; Kimi K2's low accuracy may reflect format failure.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: no support for using stated confidence alone to decide whether to trust the first answer. Pair it with a regularity check (known problem type, checkable feedback) or agreement across samples.

source: McDowell and Jacobs (2017) Meta-analysis of the effect of natural frequencies on Bayesian reasoning (Psychological Bulletin)
finding: Natural-frequency formats help Bayesian reasoning, but short-menu formats and visual aids help both formats, and method choices change performance. The effect is real but more conditional than early claims.
numbers: 35 articles, 226 performance estimates, bivariate mixed-effects model. Short menu formats and visual aids had the strongest moderation effects. Exposure to both formats also changed rates.
limits: Only the abstract was read (Europe PMC); effect sizes not extracted. No LLM content.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 partly closed: the frequency format is supported in direction. For the agent, restate probabilities as counts out of 1,000 with a small table; no LLM test found.

source: Incentivization and the conjunction fallacy in judgments: a meta-analysis (Psychological Research, 2023)
finding: The conjunction fallacy is only slightly reduced by pay for correct answers. Most single studies find no effect, but pooled there is a small one.
numbers: n = 3,276. Pooled d = 0.19; odds ratio 1.40 for a correct answer when incentivised. No moderation by payoff size.
limits: Abstract only (Europe PMC). Measures incentives, not natural frequencies or a large preregistered replication of Linda rates.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 stays open for a large replication of Linda rates. A small incentive effect suggests the error is not mainly carelessness.

source: Gan et al. (2026) BiAxisBias: Evaluating LLM Bias Beyond a Single Prompt and a Single Explanation
finding: Bias scores change with wording and with whether you read the answer or the explanation. Wording variation adds instability beyond resampling noise. This is social-stereotype bias, not heuristics-and-biases tasks.
numbers: 8 LLMs, 401 templates, 641,600 responses. Instability with three wordings 10.5% vs 6.3% for three identical calls (all ten subsets exceed control). Pair-level wording disagreement 7.00% vs 4.17% for identical calls. 9/28 model pairs reverse across four task paradigms. Selection and rationale disagree in 34.2% of 7,959 dual-valid responses.
limits: Stereotype statements, not cognitive-bias vignettes; no human test-retest comparison.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 partly closed by analogy: single-prompt bias scores carry a few points of wording noise on top of sampling noise. Report bias over several paraphrases and repeats.

source: Talboy and Fuller (2023) Challenging the appearance of machine intelligence: Cognitive bias in LLMs and Best Practices for Adoption
finding: Five classic bias prompts were run on ChatGPT-3.5, GPT-4 and Bard in March and again in August 2023 with identical wording. Some answers flipped between sessions.
numbers: ChatGPT-3.5 used Bayes' theorem in March but gave a wrong non-Bayes answer in August. Bard gave the 10% incident rate in March but used Bayes correctly in August, and in August gave consistent answers across positive and negative framing where earlier it had been framing-sensitive. GPT-4 added in August only.
limits: One run per prompt per session; no counts or statistics; product versions changed under it.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: model updates alone change bias results within months. Pin and log the model version when reporting bias tests.
